name: Ben Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no worries. I'm not a big talker, but ask away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing computer engineering, so it's a mix of programming and digital circuits, with a lab on Wednesdays that always runs late. I rent a room in a cheap shared house near campus with two other students, Callum and Tariq. Two evenings and every other Saturday I work at Harlan Hardware, mostly on the trade counter. On Sundays I sing in the choir at my family's church and have lunch at my parents' place. My dad Nikolai is a self-employed electrician, and sometimes I ride along on a job if he needs a pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and about time people stopped panicking. At Harlan's, the guys on the trade counter would shrug, because a screw is a screw whatever the AI does. Online I'd say nothing, honestly. I don't waste my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get on with my plan. I'd finish the degree and get a decent job, and if that doesn't work out, I've got my dad's trade as a fallback. What's on my mind is the rent and the loan. I've got about two weeks of money saved and my parents can't help, so I can't afford a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hardware store job and ask to go full-time over summer. I'd keep riding along with my dad on weekends, because he pays me cash and I learn real wiring. And I'd use the AI tool for debugging every now and then, the way I do now, and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty fine. A bit of stress about money, but I'm used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've got your dad's trade as a fallback. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty serious. He started with nothing. My dad has never been out of work in thirty years, because people always need a spark. I'd rather finish the degree, but I'd be fine as an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think about you doing computing instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says it's good, as long as I come out able to do something real. He's got no time for people who talk big and can't fix a fuse. I think he's right.

say: I'd say good, about time people stopped **panicking**.
I'd say nothing online, because a screw is a screw whatever the **AI** does.
think: My plan carries on, and my dad's **trade** is a fallback.
With two weeks of savings and no family help, I can't afford a bad **month**.
do: Ask for full-time hours at the **hardware store** over summer.
Keep riding along with my dad on weekends for cash and **real wiring**.
Use AI for debugging now and then, nothing more.
feel: **Fine**, with a bit of money stress I'm used to.
S0.quote: My dad has never been out of work in thirty years, because people always need a spark.
fieldNote: Calm is partly real, built on his **father's trade** as a safety net, and partly stoic.
Money is thin: two weeks saved, no family help.
Respects **practical** skill over talk, a family value from his father.

steps.text: Ask Harlan Hardware for full-time hours over the summer
Ride along on my dad's electrical jobs for cash
Put a set amount from each pay into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about time people learned to work with it and stopped complaining. I'd use it more at uni, which most of my mates already do. At Harlan's I'd tell the manager, Dennis, that stock ordering and price checks would be easy for a bot to handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think junior programming jobs shrink, because the tools write the routine code. But somebody has to understand how a system works, and computer engineering is closer to hardware than most computing degrees. That's why I picked it over pure software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a placement year, and I'd target embedded systems firms, the sort that put software into machines. I'd use AI tools properly in my coursework, as long as I understand what I hand in. And I'd talk to my dad about doing his electrical exam later on, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, not scared. If I'm useful, I'll be fine. If I'm not, that's on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if you're not useful, that's on you. Is that fair to everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not everyone. Some people don't have a dad with a van and a trade, but hard work and skills still get you a place. I'd rather say that than blame the system for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help people who lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families, first, and employers who train people. Then government for the ones who've got no one. I'm not against help, but I think it should come with a reason to work.

say: I'd say it's time people learned to **work with** it and stopped complaining.
I'd tell Dennis at Harlan's that price checks and **stock ordering** are easy for a bot.
think: Junior programming jobs shrink, but **computer engineering** sits closer to hardware.
Someone has to understand how the **system** works.
do: Go for a **placement year** at an embedded systems firm.
Use AI properly in coursework, making sure I understand every line.
Ask my dad about the electrical exam as a **backup**.
feel: **Alert**, not scared; if I'm useful, I'll be fine.
S1.quote: Some people don't have a dad with a van and a trade, but hard work and skills still get you a place.
fieldNote: Believes in **self-reliance**, yet admits his father's trade gives him an advantage others lack.
Wants help tied to **work**: families, employers, then government.
Chose computer engineering over pure software because it sits close to hardware.

steps.text: Apply for a placement year at embedded systems firms
Use an AI coding assistant on coursework and read every line
Ask my dad about the electrical qualification as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and the big firms have got to take responsibility, but they won't. And I'd tell my mates to stop waiting for someone to sort it out. At Harlan's I'd say the trade counter might be safest, because robots don't come until 2031 for hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my degree may be worth less than my dad's trade, which isn't something I thought I'd say. By 2029, when I'd finish, the thinking jobs would be mostly gone. The hands-on jobs have maybe two more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and do my electrical qualification with my dad, probably alongside my degree, or instead of it if I had to. I'd work every shift I could at Harlan's and save. And I'd learn every AI tool going so I can use it in the trade, since scheduling and quoting would all change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly anxious. I'm not a worrier, and this would make me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave the degree for the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to it, yes. My pride might take a hit, but a trade is a trade. My dad would be quietly pleased, though he'd never say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on has two extra years. Does that feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's not enough to feel safe, but it's enough to get ahead of people who didn't think of it. After that, I'd be the one who knows how to work with the machines and the wiring. That's still a place to stand.

say: I'd say the government and big firms must take **responsibility**, but they won't.
I'd tell mates to stop waiting for someone to **sort it out**.
think: My degree may be worth less than my dad's **trade**, which I never expected to say.
By 2029 the thinking jobs would be mostly gone and hands-on work has about two more **years**.
do: Start the **electrical qualification** with my dad, alongside or instead of the degree.
Work every shift at Harlan's and save.
Learn every AI tool going for quoting and scheduling.
feel: Properly **anxious**; I'm not a worrier and this would make me one.
S2.quote: My degree may be worth less than my dad's trade, which isn't something I thought I'd say.
fieldNote: Pride yields to **practicality**: he would pause the degree for the electrical qualification.
Finds his father's trade, once a fallback, suddenly **first choice**.
Calls himself not a worrier, and says this scenario would turn him into one.

steps.text: Start the electrical qualification with my dad this year
Work every extra shift at Harlan Hardware and save
Learn AI tools for quoting and scheduling electrical jobs
Pause the degree if no placement comes up by spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if you stop talking and start doing. I'd tell my mates to pick up a real skill alongside their degree, and I'd say that to my sister too. At church, someone would ask what I'd do, and I'd say I'm doing a degree and a trade at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree in 2029, and have until 2034 before the hands-on side changes much. With the degree and an electrical ticket together, I think I'd have more options than most. I'd say I'm cautious, not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the placement year and an electrical apprenticeship in my breaks, working with my dad. I'd keep the hardware store job part-time and save as much as I can. I'd use AI tools for the paperwork, quoting and design side of things, since that's where they'd help my dad most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. There's a plan, and I like plans that involve work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a degree and an electrical ticket together matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because most electricians can't program a controller, and most programmers can't wire one. A person who can do both is rare. It's the sort of job that needs someone on site, with a head for software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad react to you doing both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be proud, though he'd tell me I'm making it too complicated. He'd probably let me take on the quoting side of his business, which would save him time and teach me how a firm is run.

say: I'd say five years is enough time if you stop **talking** and start doing.
I'd tell mates and my sister to pick up a real **skill** alongside their degree.
think: With a degree and an electrical ticket I'd have more **options** than most.
I'd finish the degree in 2029 with hands-on work safe until about **2034**.
do: Do the **placement year** and an electrical apprenticeship in my breaks.
Keep the hardware store job part-time and save.
Use AI for quoting and design paperwork for my dad's business.
feel: **Steady**; there's a plan, and I like plans that involve work.
S3.quote: Most electricians can't program a controller, and most programmers can't wire one.
fieldNote: Five years lets his plan become a **dual skill**: degree plus electrical qualification.
Wants to take on the **quoting** side of his father's firm to learn how a business runs.
Steady, plan-driven, and clearly proud of his father's trade.

steps.text: Do an electrical apprenticeship during my breaks
Use AI tools to speed up quotes for my dad's firm
Save a fixed amount each pay while working part-time
Take over the quoting side of my dad's business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will waste it. I'd tell my sister to learn something she can do with her hands, and I'd tell my mates the same. At church I'd probably say it's in God's hands and we should work hard anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd finish the degree, work a few years, maybe take over some of my dad's business and grow it with software. When the big change comes, I'd have a degree, a trade and some savings. That's a decent position to be in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do a placement, get a first job and keep the electrical side going. I'd start saving properly once I'm earning, with a share going into a pension, which I'd do more than most my age. I'd use AI tools more as they get reliable, since I'm not an early adopter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd still check my bank balance, but I'd feel like I've got time to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said most people will waste ten years. What would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set small goals each year. Year one, finish first year with good marks. Year two, placement. Year three, the electrical ticket. It sounds dull, but small steps are how my dad built his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you like your life to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent job in embedded engineering, some of my own jobs on the side, a house with a garden, and, one day, a family. Nothing fancy.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will **waste** it.
I'd tell my sister and mates to learn something with their **hands**.
think: I'd finish the degree, work a few years and maybe grow my dad's business with **software**.
I'd end up with a degree, a trade and some **savings**.
do: Finish the degree, do a placement and keep the **electrical side** going.
Start a pension once I'm earning.
Adopt AI tools as they become reliable.
feel: **Calm**; I'd feel I've got time to be sensible.
S4.quote: Small steps are how my dad built his business.
fieldNote: Ten years suits his **small-steps** nature: year one marks, year two placement, year three electrical ticket.
The only scenario in which his mood is **calm**, because he has a degree, a trade and time.
Life goal is traditional and modest: a house, a garden, a family.

steps.text: Follow a yearly plan: marks, placement, electrical ticket
Start a pension from my first graduate pay
Finish the electrical qualification by year three
Adopt AI tools once they prove reliable in my placement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years doesn't give a first-year like me time to build a trade and a degree together, and the thinking jobs would go first. What would help is more apprenticeships, employers who train people instead of just hiring, and lower fees for people who study something practical.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that being independent is great until it isn't. I've got a lot of pride about not asking for help, and I know I'd have to swallow it if things went wrong. I'd rather say that now.

headlineQuote: I've got a lot of pride about not asking for help, and I know I'd have to swallow it if things went wrong.
portrait: **Ben** is an eighteen-year-old computer engineering student who works at a hardware store and rides along on his dad's electrical jobs.
He's traditional and practical, believes in self-reliance and prefers **training** and apprenticeships to handouts.
His father's **trade** is his safety net, and in the fast scenario it becomes his first choice.
He uses AI tools now and then, and his mood runs from uneasy to anxious, with calm only at ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because two years is too little to build a trade and a degree together.
whatWouldHelp: More **apprenticeships**, employers who train, and lower fees for people who study something practical.
